description: Science presented in a new way
summary:
Aéter is a web application with a built-in virtual medical assistant designed to facilitate monitoring tasks and to guide astronauts through any emergency when a specialist is not immediately available. To fulfill its function, this tool relies on NASA databases to ground its protocols and its interpretation of health data.

Our proposal includes constant monitoring of the astronaut, alerts in case of abnormalities (with an SOS option for critical situations), and assistance through super intelligence, with protocols and support during a variety of medical situations, along with a history of the actions taken and the medical record of each crew member.

On long-distance, long-duration missions there will be communication delays and a doctor will not always be on board. This project is relevant because it uses real NASA data and makes it more accessible and useful, while also being used to facilitate other essential tasks on board or in analog training scenarios.
details:
Aéter is a voice-enabled virtual medical assistant and health-monitoring dashboard for astronauts on long missions, where help from Earth arrives with a delay.

The app has five sections. Status greets the astronaut and shows the time, an SOS button, an “Alerts and Reminders” panel and a “Protocol to follow” panel, where step-by-step guidance appears during an emergency. Vitals show heart rate, blood pressure (systolic and diastolic), oxygen saturation, body temperature and respiratory rate, with live charts and dotted lines marking the warning thresholds. Aéter is the assistant: the astronaut can type or press “Talk” and speak. It answers health questions and matches emergencies, such as a seizure or tachycardia, to a protocol from a knowledge base, showing the steps. Journal lets the astronaut record how they feel each day, by writing or by telling Aéter, and keeps dated entries with summaries. History keeps a general log of conversations and the protocols shown.

A simulator generates continuous vital-sign readings for three astronaut profiles. Rules with warning and critical thresholds evaluate each reading and raise alerts. Every astronaut has a medical record with allergies, conditions, current medications and personal data. Aéter, powered by a large language model and a protocol knowledge base, reads that record together with the live vitals and active alerts, so its advice is personalized: it checks allergies and current medications before suggesting any medication, and takes the astronaut’s history into account when it guides an emergency. If no AI key is available, it falls back to local protocols. The AI also creates reminders for the astronaut, which appear in the Alerts and Reminders panel.

Aéter helps astronauts notice health problems early: every vital sign is checked against warning and critical thresholds, and any deviation is flagged right away with a clear color-coded alert instead of waiting for someone to review the numbers. When something goes wrong, it gives guided first-response steps, shown in a dedicated protocol panel, in the moments when Earth cannot answer immediately because of communication delay. Because the assistant reads each astronaut’s medical record, its advice is personalized and safer: it checks allergies and current medications before suggesting any medication, which reduces the risk of errors under stress. Voice interaction lets astronauts ask for help hands-free, which matters in microgravity and when their hands are busy treating a crewmate. Beyond emergencies, the daily journal and AI-generated reminders support well-being and routine care, and the history log keeps a dated record of conversations and protocols, so medical staff can later review what happened. Together, these features aim to give crews greater autonomy and confidence on deep-space missions. 

While crews undergo thorough medical preparation before a mission, recalling complex protocols under extreme pressure is never easy, particularly when a pilot or specialist has to step in without being a full-time physician. By turning critical procedures into plain, immediate guidance, Aéter makes emergency response far more accessible and reliable in the heat of the moment. The same approach could also help people working in other isolated environments, particularly analog astronauts operating in remote simulation habitats, where specialized medical help is far away and crews must rely on autonomous, real-time decision-making.

Built entirely in Python 3 and Streamlit, our web application integrates a vital-signs simulator, an alert engine, and a medical knowledge retrieval assistant into a live-refreshing interface. The glass-style UI and our code-generated SVG mascot, Aéter, are crafted in HTML/CSS, while JavaScript and the browser-native Web Speech API (Chrome/Edge) enable local, hands-free voice input and spoken responses without server-side audio processing.

Data persistence for crew logs, alerts, and vital-sign histories is handled by SQLite, paired with pandas and Plotly for real-time telemetry charts. The assistant generates grounded responses using the Google Gemini API (with Anthropic Claude supported as a fallback) from a curated Markdown/YAML knowledge base of 30 protocols, 95 medications, and 23 conditions sourced from NASA and ISS medical references (see references).

Our workflow combined AI-assisted development with Claude and Claude Code, automated voice-loop testing via Playwright and Chromium, version control on GitHub, and cloud hosting on Streamlit Community Cloud. Because telemetry is simulated, the platform requires no specialized hardware, only a standard PC, microphone/speakers, and a modern browser.

We built the interface around one clear priority: total simplicity for fast, stress-free understanding during an emergency. Instead of overwhelming the crew with tiny details, the voice-first design highlights essential information in just a few large elements, paired with a friendly planet character that gives the assistant an approachable face. Looking ahead, we aim to make Aéter fully functional offline using local AI models, ensuring reliable medical support even if internet access or contact with the Deep Space Network (DSN) is temporarily lost.

This prototype is for educational and simulation purposes only. It is not a certified medical device and does not replace a doctor. To ensure the assistant provides genuinely useful, realistic guidance, our team dedicated significant effort to an exhaustive review of official space-medicine literature cross-referencing NASA and ISS clinical documentation to curate a structured, high-utility knowledge base. Even so, all included protocols and vital-sign thresholds remain illustrative examples that must undergo formal clinical validation.

The demo video and illustration was SI generated
